title: “Repeat the last move” was too vague a rule for my AI-assisted puzzle game
author: tarikul4
selftext:
I designed the rules for ECHO³ and used AI assistance during development. One piece acts a turn late. That sounds easy to specify until another piece hits a wall. What exactly should the game remember when the player presses Right and nothing on that board moves?

I chose to remember the arrow. Here’s the two-turn check I used on the opening level. Press Right, then Up. On the first turn the main piece is blocked and the delayed piece waits. On the second, the delayed piece steps right. If it waits again, the implementation is remembering motion instead of input.

That distinction matters for saving, too. You can restore every piece to the correct square and still get the next turn wrong if the stored arrow is missing. What short sequence do you use to check an ambiguous rule in your own AI-assisted game?

The playable build is free and ad-supported.

[https://getquora.com/echo3/play/](https://getquora.com/echo3/play/)

comments.author: biggdogg420
comments.body: I’d add a short check for input that happens outside the board. Press blocked Right, open and close the pause menu with the arrow keys, then press Up. The delayed piece should still go Right. That catches a different bug from saving the wrong value: a menu can consume an arrow without that arrow ever becoming a game turn.

comments.author: Fancy-Proof-9449
comments.body:
I hit the same class of bug from the other side. My game replays the player's recorded path, so I store positions rather than inputs, and the ambiguous case was a teleport. If the replay clock lands between the sample before the jump and the sample after it, interpolating gives you a point on the line between them, a place the player never stood. The copy would then walk off toward somewhere that never happened.

My short check is three steps: move, teleport, then ask for the position halfway between those two samples. The answer has to be one of the real samples, never a blend.

Your point about saves is the part people miss. Restoring what you can see is easy. The state that only matters on the next turn is what gets dropped.
